name: n02-switching
title: Circuit versus packet switching
spec: Two side-by-side panels. Left panel 'Circuit switching': two endpoints joined by a single reserved path drawn as a solid thick line, notes: 'path and bandwidth reserved before data flows', 'predictable delay and jitter', 'bandwidth idle during silence'. Right panel 'Packet switching': data cut into packets, each with a header, travelling across a mesh of devices sharing links, notes: 'each packet carries a destination in its header', 'links used efficiently', 'queues can fill and packets get dropped'. Orange highlight on the bottom line: 'Ask first: does the network reserve a path or share one?'.
anchor: ## 1. Two ways to build a network
cap: Circuit switching reserves a path, while packet switching shares links and forwards each packet by its header.

name: n02-goodput
title: Overhead and goodput
spec: A stacked horizontal bar for one 1500-byte MTU segment, left to right, with byte counts: Preamble+gap 20 B (grey), Ethernet header 14 B, IP header 20 B, TCP header 20 B, data 1460 B (big green block), FCS 4 B. Label above: '1460 + 20 + 20 + 14 + 4 + 20 = 1538 byte times'. Below three result chips: 'MTU 1500: 1460 / 1538 = 94.9%', 'MTU 9000 (jumbo): 8960 / 9038 = 99.1%', 'Tiny 64-byte frame: 84 byte times on the wire, up to 148.8 million frames per second at 100 Gb/s' (orange). Monospace for arithmetic.
cap: Headers and gaps cost about 5 percent at 1500 bytes MTU and under 1 percent with jumbo frames.

name: n02-demux
title: Demultiplexing a frame
spec: Four stacked steps top to bottom with arrows, following one frame upward from the NIC: 'Ethernet: EtherType 0x0800 -> IPv4'; 'IPv4: protocol 6 -> TCP'; 'TCP: destination port 443 -> socket bound to port 443'. At the side a lookup table of keys: EtherType 0x0800 IPv4, 0x86DD IPv6, 0x0806 ARP, 0x8100 VLAN; IP protocol 1 ICMP, 6 TCP, 17 UDP; ports 22 SSH, 53 DNS, 443 HTTPS, 4791 RoCE v2. Orange note: 'No handler matches: packet dropped, ICMP unreachable or TCP RST'. Monospace for hex values.
anchor: ### Demultiplexing: how the right code gets the bytes
cap: Each layer carries a key field that tells the receiver which code should get the payload next.

name: n02-planes
title: The three planes
spec: Three stacked horizontal bands labelled Management plane (top), Control plane (middle), Data (forwarding) plane (bottom). Each band has a job line and example chips. Management: 'configures and monitors' with SSH, REST APIs, Prometheus exporters, NETCONF/gNMI, syslog. Control: 'builds the tables' with OSPF, IS-IS, BGP, STP, ARP/ND, LACP. Data: 'moves packets at line rate: parse, lookup FIB, rewrite, queue, transmit' with switching, NAT, ACL matching. Arrow from Control labelled 'RIB best routes -> FIB' to Data. Orange note: 'What happens to traffic when the control plane fails?'.
cap: The data plane moves packets, the control plane builds the tables it uses, and the management plane configures and monitors.
